title: Fre401 Prior Condition Photo
subject: Evidence
stem: On March 4, Naomi brought a portable air compressor to James's equipment repair shop for a pressure-valve service. On March 25, she returned to collect the finished unit. While James demonstrated the repaired valve, a floor-mounted hydraulic press adjacent to the workbench released unexpectedly and struck Naomi's right shoulder. Naomi sued James for the shoulder injury. At trial, James offered a still image from the shop's security camera dated March 4, showing Naomi entering the shop with her right arm in a cloth sling. Naomi objected that the image did not prove her current injury was preexisting because people wear slings for many reasons.
call: How should the court rule on James's offer of the security camera image?

choices.A: Admit the image only if James first calls a physician to explain what wearing a shoulder sling indicates about a prior injury.
choices.B: Admit the image, because it has some tendency to show that Naomi may have had a prior shoulder condition; her explanation of why she wore the sling goes to weight, not admissibility.
choices.C: Exclude the image, because it does not conclusively establish that Naomi's current shoulder injury predated the hydraulic press incident.
choices.D: Exclude the image, because a security camera photograph can never establish the medical significance of a physical condition.

rightExplanation:
FRE 401 sets a minimal relevance threshold: evidence is relevant if it has any tendency to make a fact of consequence more or less probable. Whether Naomi's shoulder had a preexisting condition is directly consequential to causation and to damages. The March 4 security image — showing her arm in a sling three weeks before the incident — has some tendency to make that fact more probable, satisfying FRE 401. The image need not conclusively establish a prior condition, and no medical foundation is required before the judge admits it. Naomi's explanation that slings serve many purposes is a weight argument for the jury, not an admissibility bar.

---

wrongExplanations.A: Expert testimony is not a prerequisite for threshold relevance. A surveillance image can be admitted once it has any probative value; medical interpretation affects how much weight the jury assigns, not whether the image clears the admissibility threshold.
wrongExplanations.C: FRE 401 requires only "any tendency," not conclusive proof. Demanding that the image conclusively establish a prior condition imposes a sufficiency standard at the admissibility stage. This choice conflates threshold relevance with ultimate persuasion on causation — the dominant trap.
wrongExplanations.D:
No categorical rule bars security camera images from showing physical conditions. Such images are ordinary circumstantial evidence. The absolute "can never" formulation signals a false rule; distractor choices using absolute language rarely state correct MBE doctrine.
